phonemes.desc: Initial labial-velar glide [w], not modern [v] — Old Norse initial v continued Proto-Germanic *w and was still a glide in the classical period — plus short open back [ɑ], carrying the stress.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n] and a second short open [ɑ]; both vowels of Vana- are short — the manuscripts write no length mark in this name.
The rising diphthong [ɛi̯], gliding from open-mid to close front — the everyday Old Norse ei of heimr, 'home, world'.
Bilabial nasal [m] closed by a tapped or trilled [r], the masculine nominative ending of heimr, fully sounded and never reduced to a vowel.

pronunciation.approximation: 'WAH-nah-HAYM-r' — begin with a w as in 'water', keep both a's short and open, glide the -hei- as in 'hay', and finish with a light rolled r.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Vanaheimr, the compound of Vana (genitive plural of Vanir) and heimr 'home, world'; Vafþrúðnismál 39 preserves the dative í Vanaheimi.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᚢᛅᚾᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱ (u-a-n-h-i-m-i-r), the Viking-Age runic rendering, initial /w/ written with úr.

kin.label: Modern Scandinavian
kin.form: Swedish and Danish Vanahem, Modern Icelandic Vanaheimur — the learned form kept alive from the medieval corpus.

kin.label: No Germanic cognate
kin.form: The Vanir themselves are attested only in the Norse sources: no Old English or Gothic name for the kindred survives, and so no cognate realm-name exists anywhere else in Germanic.

pronunciation.note: Vanaheimr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input; the Vanir's home was never hard to type, only hard to find.

domains.title: Home of the Vanir
domains.subtitle: The Elder Gods' Country Beyond the Æsir's Fence
domains.lead: Vanaheimr — Van-home — is the homeland of the Vanir, the elder kindred of gods whom the Eddas set beside the Æsir: keepers of fertility, wealth, peace, and the magic called seiðr. The record of the realm itself is one stanza and a few sentences of prose: in Vafþrúðnismál the wise powers shape Njörðr in Vanaheimr and hand him to the Æsir as a hostage, with the promise that at the doom of the age he will come home again; Snorri adds that Njörðr was raised there, and Ynglinga saga plants the Vanir's country by the river Tanais. Everything else the tradition knows of Vanaheimr it knows through its exiles — Njörðr, Freyr, and Freyja, who live among the Æsir and remain Vanir still.

cards.name: The Wise Powers
cards.desc: The vís regin of Vafþrúðnismál 39 who shaped Njörðr in Vanaheimr — the Vanir named only by their wisdom, never by their faces.

cards.name: The Hostage Ship
cards.desc: The gísling, the pledged hostage: Njörðr ferried from Vanaheimr to the Æsir to seal the peace after the first war in the world.

cards.name: Sheaf and Fecundity
cards.desc: The Vanir's province — growth, harvest, and the wealth of fields and flocks — the powers Gullveig's burning could not destroy.

cards.name: Vanaland by the Tanais
cards.desc: Ynglinga saga's euhemerized geography: the Vanir's country beside the Vanakvísl, the river the medieval world called the Don.

symbols.name: The hostage pledge (gísling)
symbols.meaning: Njörðr's transfer to the Æsir — peace made by exchanging what each side could not bear to lose

symbols.name: The vat of the truce
symbols.meaning: The peace sealed when both kindreds spat into a single vessel, from which Kvasir was made — reconciliation given a body

symbols.name: Sheaf and ship
symbols.meaning: The Vanir's twin wealth: the harvest of the fields and the sea-borne fortune of Njörðr of Nóatún and Freyr's Skíðblaðnir

symbols.name: The seiðr-staff
symbols.meaning: The magic Freyja first taught among the Æsir, which Ynglinga saga says was Vanir custom — power the immigrants carried from home

symbols.name: The broken wall of Ásgarðr
symbols.meaning: The Vanir's victory in the field — the only force in the corpus that ever breaches the Æsir's defences by open war

mythology.lead: Vanaheimr has no myth of its own: no surviving story is set inside it, no traveller describes it, no poem is located there. Its whole mythology is told from outside, by and about the gods who left it — the hostages and immigrants through whom the Vanir entered the Æsir's world, and the war whose peace made the two kindreds one household.

myths.title: In Vanaheimr the Wise Powers Created Him
myths.text:
In the wisdom-contest with the giant Vafþrúðnir, Óðinn asks whence Njörðr came among the sons of the Æsir, he who rules so many temples and sanctuaries though he was not raised among the Æsir. The giant's answer is the realm's one great attestation: in Vanaheimr the wise powers created him and gave him to the gods as a hostage — and at the doom of the age he will come back home among the wise Vanir.

The stanza does everything at once: it names the realm, names its people the wise ones, explains Njörðr's double citizenship, and promises him a homecoming that the surviving corpus never narrates. Vanaheimr is the only divine home defined not by what happens there but by who came from there — and by who is owed a return.

myths.title: The First War in the World
myths.text:
The seeress remembers the world's first war, and it begins inside the Æsir's own hall: Gullveig — the thrice-burned, thrice-born witch whom the Vanir sent or the Æsir harboured — is speared and burned in Hárr's hall, yet lives. Then the gods took counsel on whether the Æsir should pay tribute, and when battle was joined it was the Vanir who broke the wall of Ásgarðr and trod the field in victory — the seeress calls them the war-wise people, vígspá Vǫr.

No poem says who won in the end, and the silence is the point: the war could not be won. What follows in every account is not conquest but exchange — the peace that can only be made by giving hostages. Vanaheimr enters the mythology as the country strong enough to stalemate heaven and wise enough to settle it.

myths.title: The Hostage Exchange
myths.text:
Snorri and the Ynglinga tradition tell the peace from both sides. The Vanir gave their foremost: Njörðr, raised in Vanaheimr, and with him his son Freyr. The Æsir gave Hœnir, tall and comely and thought fit to be a chieftain, and with him Mímir, wisest of men, and Kvasir, wisest of the gods. When Hœnir proved helpless in council without Mímir at his shoulder, the Vanir reckoned themselves cheated — and they cut off Mímir's head and sent it to Óðinn, who preserved it with herbs and spells and consults it to this day for the hidden lore it tells him.

So the exchange that sealed the peace also seeded its bitterness. Njörðr and Freyr thrived among the Æsir and became so naturalized that Lokasenna's Loki must remind Njörðr he was only ever a hostage sent from the east. Mímir's head became Óðinn's oracle. The Vanir kept their country; the Æsir kept the immigrants; and the corpus keeps the asymmetry forever unreconciled.

myths.title: Vanaland by the Tanais
myths.text:
Snorri's Heimskringla opens its euhemerized geography with the river the medieval world called the Tanais — the Don — flowing between the peoples, and names the country on its eastern side Vanaland or Vanaheimr, and the river itself Vanakvísl. Here the mythic homeland becomes a border province of legendary history, the starting point of the migration that will carry Óðinn's people north to Sweden and set the Yngling kings at Uppsala.

The move is characteristic of the Icelandic historians: every otherworld is also a country, every god also a king. Yet even euhemerized, the pattern holds — Vanaheimr remains the place one leaves to found dynasties elsewhere, the eastern home whose children rule in the west and never quite stop being foreigners.

lore.syncretism: Vanaheimr's interpretive life is the Vanir problem itself: why does one mythology keep two divine kindreds? Dumézil made the pairing the cornerstone of his comparative system — the Æsir holding sovereignty and war, the Vanir fecundity and wealth, their war and merger the mythic charter of a complete pantheon, with structural cousins in the Roman pairing of Jupiter's Di Indigetes with the immigrant Di Novensides and in the intermarriage of cosmic orders across the Indo-European record. Current handbooks are cooler: Simek, Orchard, and Lindow note that the Vanir are attested only in the Norse sources — no Old English or Gothic trace of the kindred survives — that the Æsir/Vanir boundary blurs in practice (Skaði is a giant's daughter numbered among the goddesses; Njörðr's children outshine their host kindred), and that the war's mythology may encode history, ritual, or pure narrative logic in proportions no source will let us measure. What stands cleanly is the corpus's own testimony: two kindreds, one war, one exchange, and a homeland that keeps its identity through its exiles.
lore.culturalLegacy: Vanaheimr's modern life follows the Vanir's. Nineteenth-century philology made the Æsir–Vanir war a scholarly crux — historicized as a memory of clashing cults, read by Dumézil as structural myth — and the debate remains the standard introduction to how hard it is to get history out of the Eddas. Modern Heathenry restored the kindred to practice: Vanatrú names a living devotional current centred on Njörðr, Freyr, and Freyja as gods of peace, fertility, and the household's wealth, with Vanaheimr honoured as their true home. Popular culture adopted the realm as scenery: Marvel's Thor comics placed Vanaheim among the Nine Realms and carried it onto film, and Santa Monica Studio's God of War Ragnarök (2022) rendered it as a vast jungle river-world — depictions with no warrant in the medieval record, which gives the realm no landscape at all. The restoration keeps the plain compound the sources actually wrote: the Vanir's home, named once in a wisdom-contest and remembered ever since.
lore.extendedMeditation: Every heimr in the Norse cosmos is a homestead, but Vanaheimr is the one defined by leaving it. Ásgarðr has its walls and halls, Miðgarðr its fence, Jötunheimr its giants; Vanaheimr has a departure and a promise. The wise powers shape Njörðr and hand him over, and the corpus never once takes us back across the border — we know the realm only as the place the hostage came from, the address on a homecoming that Ragnarǫk will finally honour. There is something exact in that economy: a peace that could only be made by each side surrendering what it could least spare, and a god who spends his whole mythic life as a guest in someone else's heaven, ruling temples among the Æsir while remaining, at the level of grammar and fate, a Vanir abroad. Vanaheimr is the mythology's quietest lesson in what homes are for: not to be described, but to be owed a return.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Vanaheimr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚢᛅᚾᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱ (u-a-n-h-i-m-i-r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: vanaheimr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 39 (Njörðr created in Vanaheimr by the wise powers and given as hostage; the promised homecoming); Völuspá 21–24 (Gullveig and the first war; the Vanir break the wall of Ásgarðr); Lokasenna 34 (Njörðr taunted as a hostage sent from the east)

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 23 (Njörðr raised in Vanaheimr, given as hostage to the Æsir; his marriage to Skaði; Freyr and Freyja his children); Skáldskaparmál (kennings for Njörðr as god of the Vanir)
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 1 and 4 (Vanaland/Vanaheimr by the river Vanakvísl-Tanais; the Æsir–Vanir war and the hostage exchange; the beheading of Mímir)
Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum IV.26–27 (the temple at Uppsala and the cult image of Fricco-Freyr) — the Vanir cult's contemporary material testimony
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. Vanir, heimr; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. Vanir, heimr
de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, s.v. Vanir (the contested etymology: connections proposed with vinr 'friend' and Latin Venus, none secure)
Dumézil, Gods of the Ancient Northmen (the Æsir–Vanir pairing as the structural charter of sovereignty and fecundity)

Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology; Orchard, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend; Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide — s.v. Vanaheimr, Vanir, Njörðr (attestation, the Vanir problem, and the limits of reconstruction)

lore.archaeology: A realm named once in a wisdom-contest can leave no votives: Vanaheimr's evidence is manuscript evidence. Vafþrúðnismál and Völuspá survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270); Snorri's Gylfaginning and the Heimskringla tradition transmit the prose attestations. No runic inscription names Vanaheimr, and none names the Vanir as a kindred — a silence the realm shares with most of the cosmological furniture. The material record belongs to the Vanir's cult rather than their home: Adam of Bremen's description (c. 1070s) of the temple at Uppsala, where the idol Fricco — Freyr — stood between Wodan and Thor, fashioned with an immense phallus as the god of peace and pleasure; and the dense stratum of Scandinavian place-names compounded with Njörðr and Freyr (Swedish Närlunda from Njarðarlundr, Frøslev, Frösåker and their kin), which maps the kindred's worship across the landscape even where the mythology is silent. The Yngling dynasty's claimed descent from Yngvi-Freyr ties that cult geography to the great burial mounds of Gamla Uppsala — the closest the earth comes to showing us Vanaheimr's people.
